newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Jan 31.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Jan 31.

text.p: The government and the Serious Fraud Office will hold separate investigations into Aotearoa Television Network. The cabinet agreed on Monday to give the Maori television station in Auckland $4 million to keep it afloat till June -- $2 million from the public broadcasting fee; the remaining $2 from taxpayers. However, Prime Minister Jim Bolger, Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters and senior officials met on Thursday morning and decided the money would be put on hold till the government was satisfied Aotearoa Television's finances were above board. Page 1.

Serious Fraud Office assistant John Hicks defended a suggestion at the commission of inquiry into Cook Islands tax deals on Thrusday that the office deliberately set out to mislead Auckland businessman Stephen Lunn. Commission lawyer Colin Carruthers, QC, asked Hicks during cross-examination: "What do you see as the justification for an office called the SFO to be making statements that are misleading?" "I don't regard it as serious misleading," Hicks said. "I regard it as tactics more than misleading." Page2.

Four Chinese seismologists have arrived in New Zealand to test earthquake forecasting theories. The Chinese, acknowledged as world leaders in forecasting earthquakes, have had mixed successes. Their forecasting procedures incorporate information gathered from a huge monitoring programme combining comprehensive scientific and computing analyses with local expertise and experience. THe team in New Zealand is interested in exploring computer models for risk estimates developed by Victoria University scientist David Vere-Jones. Page 2.

The four main industry groups have turned down the coalition government's plan to spend an extra $100 million on business assistance. The Chambers of Commerce, Employers Federation, Federated Farmers and the Manufacturers Federation are all concerned about the government's higher spending plans and the likely impact on inflation. The coalition agreement involved an extra $1.2 billion in government spending in the next financial year. Page 11.

Speculation that its share price is undervalued, the New Zealand dollar is overvalued and a persistent takeover rumour have sent Lion Nation's share price on an undulating ride this week. The takeover rumour stems from talk around the traps that international tobacco, food and brewing conglomerate, Philip Morris, through brewing subsidiary Miller Brewing Co, is after Lion chief executive Doug Myers' 16 percent holding of Lion at up to $4.60 a share. Page 11.

Vegetable processor Cedenco will return to the High Court at Auckland on February 10 for closing evidence and submissions in a $3.046 million claim against State Insurance for unpaid insurance on crops ruined by rain in late 1992 and early 1993. State will call two more witnesses before both parties give closing submissions in what promises to be a benchmrk case for the insurance industry. Page 11.

The December quarter Household Labour Force Survey due on Tuesday and wage data later next month will be the most important factors for the Reserve Bank's March economic forecasts other than the changes to the fiscal settings, Bankers Trust says. Other indicators, such as the ANZ job ads and registered unemployed, pointed to a further slowdown in employment growth, chief economist David Plank said. Page 11.

A leading Wellington department store, Kirkcaldie and Stains, had a late Christmas rush, enjoyed "buoyant trading" in January and expects the present full-year profit to top last year's result. At the company's annual meeting in Wellington on Thursday, managing director Philip Shewell said pre-Christmas trading was ahead of the same period in 1995 and was "far better" than expected in early December. Page 11.
